FEEDS: Weak and rare. Overfed succulents stretch, go soft, then rot.
Stop the moment nights drop under 15°C.
The hungriest thing you will own. Top-dress 1 cm vermicompost monthly.
Half strength, or seaweed on its own
Every 10 days while you are picking
Harvesting is what drives regrowth. Feed after each cut.
Bark holds no nutrients, so little and often beats a big dose.
Switch to a bloom feed the moment buds appear.
No fertiliser and no tap water. Rain or RO only, or they die.

DEFIC.sym: Whole leaf pales to uniform yellow-green, starting at the bottom of the plant and moving up. Growth slows, stems thin.
DEFIC.fix: Any balanced feed, or 19:19:19 at 3 g/L. Fastest organic route is fermented mustard-cake liquid.
DEFIC.here: Common in coco-heavy mixes, which hold almost no nitrogen of their own.

DEFIC.sym: Dull dark green going purple or bronze, especially on leaf undersides and stems. Few flowers, poor root growth.
DEFIC.fix: Bone meal or SSP worked into the top two inches, or 0:52:34 at 5 g/L as a spray.
DEFIC.here: Often a pH problem rather than a shortage — above 7.5 phosphorus locks into insoluble calcium compounds.

DEFIC.sym: Leaf edges scorch brown and curl while the centre stays green. Weak stems, fruit that will not sweeten.
DEFIC.fix: 13:0:45 at 4 g/L, or wood ash worked in. Every fruiting plant needs more K than it is usually given.
DEFIC.here: The classic mistake is feeding nitrogen through the fruiting phase — you get a magnificent plant and no crop.

DEFIC.sym: Yellow between the veins while the veins themselves stay sharply green. Starts low on the plant.
DEFIC.fix: Epsom salt at 5 g/L, as a drench or a foliar spray. Visible improvement in about ten days.
DEFIC.here: Very common in high-potassium feeding regimes — K and Mg compete for uptake.

DEFIC.sym: Yellow between the veins with a fine green vein network, on the youngest growth. Severe cases go near-white.
DEFIC.fix: Chelated iron (EDDHA form above pH 7) at 2 g/L. Correct the pH as well or it returns.
DEFIC.here: The signature coal-belt deficiency. Fly-ash deposition pushes soil alkaline and iron stops being available. Citrus and jaboticaba show it first.

DEFIC.sym: Growing tips die back. In fruit, a sunken black patch at the blossom end of tomato, chilli and capsicum.
DEFIC.fix: Gypsum or crushed eggshell in the mix. Calcium nitrate at 2 g/L for a fast correction.
DEFIC.here: Blossom end rot is almost never a calcium shortage — it is a watering shortage. Calcium travels in the transpiration stream, so a pot that swings wet-dry cannot deliver it however much you add.

DEFIC.sym: Small, narrow, bunched leaves with shortened internodes — a rosette at the shoot tip.
DEFIC.fix: Zinc sulphate at 2 g/L foliar, or any chelated micronutrient mix.
DEFIC.here: Frequent in mango and citrus on alkaline soil. Worth including in the monthly micronutrient spray rather than waiting for symptoms.

DEFIC.sym: Brittle, distorted new leaves, hollow or corky fruit, poor fruit set despite heavy flowering.
DEFIC.fix: Borax at 0.5 g/L, no more. Boron is the easiest nutrient to overdose into toxicity.
DEFIC.here: Shows up as flower drop on chilli and brinjal that gets misread as a pollination failure.

DEFIC.sym: Uniform pale yellow on the youngest leaves — looks like nitrogen shortage but at the wrong end of the plant.
DEFIC.fix: Any sulphate-form fertiliser, or elemental sulphur, which also corrects pH.
DEFIC.here: Rare, but the confusion with nitrogen is common. Check which leaves are affected before treating.

NPKS.why: Balanced and fully water-soluble. The default feed for anything that is growing but not yet fruiting.
High potassium, no phosphorus. Switch to it the day flowers open on tomato, chilli, papaya or guava.

NPKS.rate: 5 g/L, two sprays two weeks apart
NPKS.why: Mono-potassium phosphate. Pushes a mature mango from vegetative growth into flowering.

NPKS.when: Two to three weeks after transplant
NPKS.why: High phosphorus. Use once at establishment, not repeatedly — phosphorus accumulates and locks out zinc and iron.

NPKS.when: Fruit set on tomato and capsicum
NPKS.why: Also what you charge coco peat with. Never mix it in the same can as a phosphate or sulphate feed — it precipitates.
Cheap, safe, and fixes the commonest interveinal yellowing on old leaves.

ORGIN.d: Slow, safe, and it carries the microbial life that makes the rest work. The base of every mix here.
Nitrogen plus genuine nematode and grub suppression. Must be composted or well mixed — fresh cake burns roots.
Cake 1:10 in water, fermented ten days, then diluted 1:10 again. It will smell. The fastest organic nitrogen available.
Slow-release phosphorus and calcium. Works only in acid to neutral mix — above pH 7.5 it does almost nothing.
Free potash. But it is strongly alkaline — skip it entirely if your mix already tests above 7.5.
Not a fertiliser. Growth hormones and micronutrients that improve heat and transplant tolerance — worth it for May.
Bulk and structure more than nutrition. Fresh dung burns and carries weed seed — it must be at least six months old.

PHBANDS.d: Phosphorus, calcium and magnesium become unavailable. Aluminium turns toxic.
Everything available. Target this for tomato, chilli, citrus, guava, jaboticaba.
Slight iron and manganese reduction. Acceptable for mango, jamun, sapota.
Interveinal yellowing on new growth. Adding more iron sulphate will not fix it — use EDDHA chelate.
Iron, manganese, zinc, boron and phosphorus all unavailable. Feeding harder does literally nothing.

FEEDCAL.d: Minimal feeding. Root-prune woody pots. Zone C crops still cropping — keep the high-K going there only.
Growth restarts. Resume 19:19:19 fortnightly. Mango at bloom: no nitrogen, sulphur spray for mildew.
Full feeding on everything outdoors. Last month before heat. Micronutrient spray.
Halve rates. Salts concentrate fast in bags that are drying twice a day.
Feed nothing. A plant at 45°C is not growing, and unused salts burn roots. Flush every bag once with plain water.
First rain, first flush. Restart at half rate, build over three weeks.
Best growing month. Full rates, plus FYM top-dress. Nitrogen-led for juvenile trees.
Continue. Nothing newly potted gets fed for 3–4 weeks after the move.
Second flush. Micronutrients. Start the seedling programme on quarter-strength only.
Mango year 3+: two sprays of 0:52:34 for flower initiation. Zone C transplants get their first feed.
Switch every flowering plant to 13:0:45. Stop nitrogen on anything setting fruit.
High-K only, on croppers. Mango: withhold water and feed to set up the February bloom.

FEEDDONT: Water first, feed thirty minutes later. Fertiliser on dry roots burns them — this is the commonest way people kill a plant while trying to help it.
Wilting, scorched, or repotted within four weeks. A cut root system cannot use fertiliser; it can only be damaged by it.
Salts concentrate in a fast-drying fabric bag. Flush instead.
Never mix calcium with phosphate or sulphate
In the same watering can they precipitate into a useless white sludge. Separate applications, days apart.
Doubling the dose does not double growth. It raises salt concentration until the roots lose water to the soil instead of gaining it — the leaf symptoms look exactly like drought.
Above 7.8 most micronutrients are chemically unavailable regardless of how much you apply.

sym: White or tan crust on the mix surface or the bag rim
Leaf tips and margins browning on many plants at once
Growth stalls while the plant looks otherwise healthy
Water runs through faster than it used to
fix: Take the bag somewhere it can drain freely
Pour slow, plain water equal to twice the bag volume through it — 150 L through a 75 L bag
Let it drain fully, then leave it a week before feeding again
Repeat every 4–6 months on any bag that has been fed all season
